monument_type: Pillar, Courtyard building, Shrine, Archaeological object(s)
description_en: Kanakāsundarī Temple, one kilometre east of Hatsinja village and near Sahubada settlement, is built on the south-eastern end of a rocky hill dominating Sahubada village. The rocky hill has been identified as the capital of the Khaśa Malla kingdom, which existed between the 12th and 14th centuries (Tucci 1956andAndolfatto 2019). According to Tibetan sources, the area is the capital of Yatse (tib. ya rste), or Yatse itself, the name of the Khaśa Malla kingdom. Following the collapse of the Khaśa Malla polity, Sinja remained an important centre of power under the Kalyāl dynasty (Pant 2009and Andolfatto 2019).The central Temple, built in the centre of a quadrangular compound, is dedicated to the goddess Kanakāsundarī. It is a square stone construction with mud mortar and wooden chaining. Metal shingles are used to cover the hip roof. The only exit is on the north-western side. It is framed by large stone blocks and, a mid-14th century stone memorial pillar has been repurposed as a lintel. A narrow platform runs around the monument's walls. It contains a variety of objects of varying antiquity. The two stone lions on either side of door are probably the most iconic objects (JUM0430-001 and 002).The four wings that surround the Kanakāsundarī Temple contain storage rooms for rituals and cooking, among other things. There are four shrines on each corner of the quadrangle: To the west is Kālikā, Lāmā to the north, Jālapā to the east and Nārāyaṇa to the south. Lāmā is a significant local deity, whose legend indicates that he is of Tibetan origin (Unbescheid 1987andYasuno 2018). His main temple is in the village of Lekhpur (JUM0540), about a few hours walk to the south-east.A Kafle clan from Deharpata in the Sinja Valley performs rituals at the Temple. The goddess is part of the local group of Navadurgā Bhavānī. One version of her legend, collected in Sinja in 2018 CE, goes as follows:"Long ago the king had a servant in charge of the kitchens. Every day this servant gave some rice to a poor woman before the king. One day the king realised that he was not being served first. He thought it was the cook who was being served. The cook learned of the king's suspicions and, lest the king become angry, he explained that a woman had come to beg for his food. The king decided to find out for sure. The next day he hid and observed the scene for himself. When the king saw the woman receiving food before him, he became angry and wanted to grab her. But the woman turned to stone and from that moment on everything went wrong in the kingdom. A temple was built to put an end to it. It is because the woman was fed raw broken rice (kanikā), that her name is Kanakāsundarī." (published inAndolfatto 2019, see alsoYasuno 2018for an alternative version).

historical_events.event_description: The lintel of the main temple's door is a repurposed stone memorial pillar. The pillar's typology dates it to the mid-14th century. Astūpais carved on the top of the pillar and a heavily eroded inscription written in Nāgarī script can be seen beneath thestūpa. Posterior to this original inscription are other more recent inscriptions and carvings, such as the central arch with round decorative patterns. To the right is a more legible inscription with the date 1976 (on the image). This date corresponds to 1919 CE when expressed in the Vikram era.
